7840:
"Hold out for" means to refuse to accept something until you get exactly what you want.

When you "hold out for" something, you are saying:

"No, I will not take what you are offering me right now. I will wait. I will be patient. I will only say yes when I get the specific thing I want."

So there are two key ideas working together here:

  1. You are being offered something, but you are refusing it.
  2. You are waiting specifically for something better — something particular that you have in your mind.
A Simple Picture to Understand It

Imagine you are selling your old bicycle. Someone offers you $50. You know it is worth $100. So you say, "No, thank you," and you keep waiting until someone pays you $100.

You are holding out for $100.

You are not giving up. You are not accepting less. You are standing firm and waiting for what you truly want.

The pattern is simple:

hold out for + [the thing you want]

Here are clean examples:

  • She is holding out for a better job offer.
  • He held out for more money.
  • Don't hold out for a perfect moment — it may never come.
  • They are holding out for a house with a garden.
  • I held out for the exact color I wanted and finally found it.

Notice that "hold out for" is always followed by a noun or noun phrase — the specific thing you are waiting or hoping to get.

This phrase carries three hidden ideas inside it that you must feel, not just know:

1. Refusal
You are actively saying no to what is being offered right now. This is not passive waiting. This is a deliberate choice to reject the current offer.

2. Patience and persistence
You are willing to wait — even if it takes a long time — because you believe what you want is worth waiting for.

3. Risk
This is the most important hidden idea. When you hold out for something, there is always a risk that you might end up with nothing at all. The offer you refused might not come back. The better deal might never arrive. This risk is almost always present in the background of this phrase. That's what makes holding out for something a bold or brave decision.
Real-Life Situations Where You'll Hear This Phrase

In a job or salary negotiation:

"The company offered her $70,000 a year, but she held out for $85,000 — and got it."

In buying or selling:

"He refused three offers on his house. He was holding out for the right buyer."

In sports (very common in professional sports):

"The player refused to sign the contract. He was holding out for a bigger deal."

In relationships:

"She's not dating anyone right now. She's holding out for someone who truly respects her."

In everyday decisions:

"I didn't buy any shoes on sale. I'm holding out for the exact pair I want."

When someone says, "I'm holding out for...", you should sense a person who:

  • Knows what they want
  • Is not desperate
  • Has self-belief
  • Is willing to be uncomfortable or wait rather than settle for less

The phrase is often used with admiration — as in, "Good for you for not settling." But it can also carry a warning — as in, "Don't hold out for too long, or you'll miss your chance."
"Hold Out For" vs. Words It's Confused With

"Wait for" — This just means you expect something to arrive. There's no refusal involved.

"I'm waiting for the bus." ← You didn't refuse the bus. You're simply expecting it.

"Hold out for" — You are actively refusing current options and staying firm until a specific thing comes.

"I'm holding out for a direct flight, even though cheaper connecting flights are available." ← You are saying no to the connecting flights.

"Settle for" — This is the opposite of "hold out for." When you settle for something, you accept something less than what you wanted because you got tired of waiting or felt you had no choice.

"I held out for months, but in the end I settled for a smaller apartment."

This phrase is neutral — it is perfectly natural in both casual conversation and professional settings.

  • ✅ You can say it to a friend: "Hold out for someone who treats you right."
  • ✅ You can say it in a business meeting: "We're holding out for a more favorable contract."
  • ✅ You can read it in a newspaper: "The union is holding out for a 10% wage increase."
A Memorable Way to Remember It

Think of the image of a person holding their hand out, palm up, refusing to close it around something being offered to them — waiting with an open hand until something better lands in it.

Holding out = not closing the deal. For = specifically waiting for this thing.
"Hold out for" means to patiently refuse to accept anything less than the specific thing you want, even if it means waiting a long time or taking a risk.
7841:
"Hold sway" means to have strong power, control, or influence over someone or something. When a person, idea, belief, or force "holds sway," it dominates — it shapes how people think, feel, or behave in a powerful and often widespread way.

Think of it like this: whoever or whatever "holds sway" is essentially in charge — not necessarily through laws or rules, but through deep influence or authority that others follow, accept, or submit to.

The key to understanding this idiom is the word "sway."

Physically, "sway" means to swing back and forth — like a tree branch swaying in the wind. The branch bends wherever the wind pushes it. This physical image gave birth to a figurative idea: if you can make things bend to your will, you have sway — you have influence and power.

Over centuries, "sway" became a word for rule or dominion, meaning the power to control or govern. So "hold sway" simply means to hold that power — to maintain a firm grip on influence or control.

The idiom has roots in Old English and Old Norse, where "sway" (from the Old Norse word sveigja, meaning "to bend or give way") gradually developed from a physical meaning into a figurative one connected to rulership and authority.

By the 16th century, "sway" was being used in English to mean dominion or rule — as in, a king who "holds sway" over his kingdom. The phrase has been a part of the English language ever since, surviving into modern usage especially in formal writing, journalism, literature, and speeches.

Structure:

The most common pattern is:

[Someone/Something] + holds sway + over + [a person, group, place, or situation]

The word "over" is very commonly used with this idiom, though it is not always required.

Here are examples across different contexts so you can see how flexible this idiom is:

About a person:

  • "For many years, the old general held sway over the entire military."

(= The general had powerful control over the military.)

About an idea or belief:

  • "In the 19th century, the belief that the Earth was only a few thousand years old still held sway among many people."

(= That belief was dominant and widely accepted.)

About an emotion:

  • "During the crisis, fear held sway over the whole nation."

(= Fear had a powerful grip on the nation; it dominated people's feelings and actions.)

About a trend or style:

  • "Before streaming services arrived, television held sway in every household."

(= Television was the dominant, most powerful form of entertainment.)

About a place:

  • "In this remote village, old traditions still hold sway."

(= Old traditions are still dominant and control how people live.)
Key Things to Understand About This Idiom

1. It implies strong, lasting, or widespread influence — not a small or temporary one.

"Hold sway" is not used for minor or fleeting influence. It suggests something that has serious power, often over a large group of people, a wide area, or a long period of time. You wouldn't say "his joke held sway over the room for a second." That's too small and brief. You'd say "his charisma held sway over the entire audience throughout his speech."

2. It can describe people, ideas, emotions, trends, forces — almost anything.

This is a very flexible idiom. The thing that "holds sway" doesn't have to be a person. It can be:

  • An ideology (e.g., democracy, religion)
  • An emotion (e.g., fear, love, hope)
  • A trend (e.g., a fashion, a technology)
  • A force of nature (e.g., "winter holds sway over the northern lands")

3. It has a slightly formal or literary tone.

You are more likely to read "hold sway" in books, newspapers, formal essays, or speeches than to hear it in everyday casual conversation. In casual speech, people might just say "dominate," "be in control," or "run the show." But "hold sway" carries a more elegant, classic weight to it.

4. The tense changes, but the idiom stays the same.

  • "holds sway" → present (currently in control)
  • "held sway" → past (was in control)
  • "will hold sway" → future (will be in control)

Don't confuse it with:

  • "Hold away" — this is not a real idiom; it's a mishearing of "hold sway."
  • "Sway someone" — this means to change someone's opinion or decision ("His speech swayed the voters"). This is different from "hold sway," which is about maintaining ongoing power or influence, not a single moment of persuasion.

These expressions are close in meaning and can help you understand "hold sway" even better by comparison:

  • "Reign supreme" — to be the most powerful or dominant ("Rock music reigned supreme in the 1980s.")
  • "Hold dominion over" — to rule over, very similar to "hold sway" but even more formal and archaic.
  • "Have a grip on" — to maintain control over something ("The dictator had a tight grip on the country.")
  • "Call the shots" — to be the one making decisions, but this is more casual and about active decision-making, less about passive influence.
  • "Be in the driver's seat" — to be in control, but again more casual.

"Hold sway" sits in a slightly more formal, grand, and literary register compared to all of these.

Picture a king standing on a throne, gently swaying a royal sceptre back and forth. Everything and everyone in the kingdom bends and follows that sway. That king holds sway — he holds the power to make the whole kingdom move according to his will.

Whenever something is so powerful that others bend to it — a ruler, a belief, a fear, a trend — it holds sway.
"Hold sway" = to have a powerful, dominant, and often lasting influence or control over people, places, situations, or ideas.
7842:
"Hold the fort" means to take care of things and keep a situation stable while someone else is temporarily away. It is used when one person leaves a place or a responsibility in someone else's hands, trusting that person to manage things until they return.

Think of it this way: if your friend runs a shop and has to step out for an hour, they might say to you, "Can you hold the fort while I'm gone?" They are asking you to make sure everything keeps running smoothly — no chaos, no problems — until they come back.

The core idea is temporary responsibility + maintaining the status quo.
Breaking It Down Word by Word

• "Hold" here means to maintain, defend, or keep control of.
  • "The fort" refers to a place or situation that needs to be protected or managed.

Together, the phrase paints a picture of someone standing guard over something important and not letting it fall apart.

This idiom has a military origin, and understanding it makes the meaning crystal clear.

A fort is a strong, enclosed military base built for defense. In battles of the past, soldiers would be ordered to hold (meaning defend and not surrender) their fort against enemy attacks. If the commander had to leave to get reinforcements, the remaining soldiers had to hold the fort — stay strong, defend the position, and not let the enemy take over — until help arrived.

The phrase became widely known during the American Civil War. In October 1864, at the Battle of Allatoona Pass, Union General William Tecumseh Sherman sent a famous signal message to his troops who were under heavy Confederate attack. The message read:

"Hold the fort, for I am coming."

He was telling his soldiers to hang on, defend their position, and not give up — he was on his way with reinforcements. This moment was so famous that it became a cultural landmark, and a popular gospel song called "Hold the Fort" (1870) by Philip Paul Bliss was even written based on it, which spread the phrase far and wide into everyday civilian life.

Over time, the phrase drifted away from warfare and into ordinary, day-to-day language — and that is exactly how idioms are born.

Today, this idiom has nothing to do with battles or soldiers. It is simply used whenever someone temporarily takes charge of a place, job, or situation while the usual person is absent.

The "fort" can be:

  • An office
  • A shop or business
  • A home
  • A project or task
  • Any ongoing responsibility

The key elements present in almost every use of this idiom are:

  1. Someone is leaving temporarily. They are not gone forever — they will return.
  2. Someone else is left in charge. That person is trusted to manage things.
  3. The goal is stability. The person holding the fort isn't expected to make big changes — just keep things going as they are.

Here are examples across different situations so you can see how naturally this idiom fits into conversation:

At work:

  • "I have a dentist appointment at noon. Can you hold the fort until I'm back around 2?"
  • "The manager is traveling this week, so David is holding the fort at the office."

At home:

  • "I need to run to the grocery store. Can you hold the fort with the kids for 30 minutes?"
  • "She held the fort at home while her husband was deployed overseas."

In business:

  • "When the CEO stepped down unexpectedly, the COO held the fort until a replacement was found."

Casual, informal use:

  • "I'm just going to step out for a bit — you hold the fort, okay?"
"Hold the Fort" vs. "Hold Down the Fort"

You will often hear people say "hold down the fort" — especially in American English. This is simply a variation of the same idiom with the same meaning. Neither version is wrong.

  • "Hold the fort" — the original, traditional form. More common in British English.
  • "Hold down the fort" — a later variation. More common in American English.

Both mean exactly the same thing: to manage and maintain a situation while others are away.

This is an informal, conversational idiom. You would use it in:

  • Everyday speech
  • Casual emails
  • Friendly workplace conversations

You would generally not use it in formal writing like legal documents, academic papers, or official reports. In those settings, you would say something like "maintain operations" or "oversee responsibilities in my absence."

It is worth clearing up what the idiom does not imply:

  • It does not mean the person is doing something heroic or dramatic. It can be as simple as watching a desk.
  • It does not mean there is any real danger involved (unlike its military origins). In modern usage, the "threat" is simply the possibility of things going wrong or unmanaged.
  • It does not imply a long period of time. It is almost always used for short or temporary absences.

QuestionAnswer

What does it mean? → To temporarily look after a place or responsibility while someone else is away.

Where did it come from? → Military language — literally defending a fort while waiting for reinforcements. Popularized by the American Civil War.

When do you use it? → In casual, everyday speech when someone is leaving a responsibility in another person's hands.

Can you say "hold down the fort"? → Yes, absolutely. It means the same thing.

The beauty of this idiom is that once you picture those soldiers holding their position, refusing to let things fall apart until help arrives — the meaning becomes unforgettable. Every time you use it in modern life, that same spirit lives on: stay steady, keep things going, and don't let it fall apart.
7843:
When something "holds true," it means that a statement, rule, fact, belief, or principle remains valid, accurate, and applicable — even when the situation changes, time passes, or new circumstances arise.

Think of the word "hold" here not as grabbing something with your hand, but as staying firm or not giving way — like how a bridge "holds" under heavy weight. It doesn't break. It stays strong. In the same way, when a statement "holds true," it doesn't break down or fall apart under new conditions. It stays correct.
The Simplest Way to Understand It

Imagine a rule that says: "Practice makes perfect."

Now, does this rule apply only to musicians? No. Does it apply only to children? No. Does it work for athletes, writers, doctors, and painters too? Yes.

So you could say:

"The idea that practice makes perfect holds true for almost every skill in life."

The statement didn't change. The world around it changed (different people, different skills, different times), but the truth of that statement held firm. It held true.
Breaking Down the Two Words

"Hold" — In this idiom, "hold" means to remain, to stay, or to continue to be. It signals that something is not weakening or disappearing. It is standing firm.

"True" — This means accurate, valid, or correct.

Put them together: "Hold true" = to continue to be accurate and valid.
The Core Idea in One Line
Something holds true when it was correct before and is still correct now, or when it applies in one place and also applies in another.
How It Is Used — The Grammar

"Hold true" is almost always used in one of these patterns:

Pattern 1: Something holds true (on its own)

"This theory no longer holds true."

(= This theory is no longer valid.)

Pattern 2: Something holds true FOR someone/something

"This advice holds true for everyone, not just beginners."

(= This advice is valid and applicable for everyone.)

Pattern 3: Something holds true IN a situation or context

"The same principle holds true in the world of business."

(= The same principle is valid in business too.)

Pattern 4: Something holds true EVEN WHEN / EVEN IF...

"This holds true even when the temperature changes."

(= This stays valid regardless of temperature change.)

Pattern 5: As a question

"Does this still hold true today?"

(= Is this still valid/accurate today?)
Real-World Examples With Explanations

Example 1:

"The laws of mathematics hold true everywhere in the universe."

Explanation: Whether you are in Paris, Tokyo, or on the moon, 2 + 2 = 4. That mathematical fact stays valid everywhere. It doesn't stop being true depending on where you are. So it "holds true" universally.

Example 2:

"What my grandfather said about patience holds true to this day."

Explanation: The grandfather said something wise, perhaps many decades ago. Even now, in a completely different era, that wisdom is still correct and still applies. The truth of what he said has not faded with time. It held true then, and it holds true now.

Example 3:

"This rule holds true for most cases, but there are a few exceptions."

Explanation: The rule is generally valid and applicable, but the speaker is being honest — it doesn't apply in every single situation. Even so, it holds true most of the time.

Example 4:

"The same principle that holds true for adults holds true for children as well."

Explanation: A principle that works for adults also works for children. It doesn't lose its correctness when applied to a different group of people.

Example 5 (negative use):

"That stereotype does not hold true in reality."

Explanation: The stereotype might seem like it's true, but when you actually look at reality, it is not valid. It does not hold true — meaning it fails, it breaks down, it is not accurate.
What "Hold True" Is NOT Saying

This idiom is not about someone personally being honest or loyal. For example:

❌ "He holds true to his word" — this is a different, related expression meaning he keeps his promises. This is "hold true to something" — a slightly different structure with a different meaning (see below).

✅ "The theory holds true" — this is the idiom we are discussing, meaning the theory remains valid.

Be careful with this distinction.
A Related Expression: "Hold True TO Something"

When you add "to" after "hold true," the meaning shifts slightly:

"She holds true to her values no matter what."

Here, it means she remains faithful and loyal to her values — she doesn't abandon them under pressure. This is about personal commitment, not about a fact being valid.

So remember:

  • "It holds true" = a fact/rule/statement remains valid and applicable.
  • "He/she holds true to something" = a person remains faithful/loyal to something.
Words That Mean the Same Thing (Synonyms)

When something "holds true," you could also say it:

  • Stands — "The argument still stands."
  • Applies — "This rule still applies."
  • Remains valid — "The theory remains valid."
  • Holds good — "This principle holds good even today." (slightly old-fashioned but still used)
  • Still rings true — "Those words still ring true." (carries more of an emotional resonance)
  • Holds up — "This claim doesn't hold up under scrutiny."
Words That Mean the Opposite (Antonyms in Context)

When something does not hold true, you can say it:

  • No longer applies
  • Has been disproven
  • Falls apart / breaks down
  • Does not hold
  • Is no longer valid
The Tone and Register — When Do People Use This?

"Hold true" is neutral and slightly formal. You will find it commonly used in:

  • Academic writing — "This conclusion holds true across multiple studies."
  • Professional discussions — "The same logic holds true in our industry."
  • Everyday thoughtful speech — "What my teacher told me still holds true today."
  • Philosophical or reflective writing — "Ancient wisdom often holds true in the modern world."

It is rarely used in very casual, slang-heavy conversation, but it is not so formal that it sounds out of place in normal speech either.
Why This Idiom Exists — The "Big Picture" Logic

Language needed a phrase to express a specific idea: the idea that truth has staying power. Not all statements are timeless. Some things are true only once, only in one place, or only for one person. But some truths are durable — they survive changing times, changing places, and changing people.

"Hold true" captures exactly that durability. The word "hold" gives a sense of strength and resistance — like something gripping tightly and not letting go. The statement doesn't just happen to be true; it actively holds onto its truth across circumstances. That's the image the idiom paints.
Quick Summary

MeaningTo remain valid, accurate, and applicable across different times, places, or situations
Key ideaSomething was true before, and it is still true now — or it is true here, and it is also true there
Common structure"[Statement] holds true (for/in/even when...)"
ToneNeutral to slightly formal
Don't confuse with"Hold true to something" = to remain faithful/loyal to something

The next time you see or hear "holds true," ask yourself: Is someone saying that a rule, fact, or principle stays valid in this new context? If yes — you've understood it perfectly.
7844: "Hold up" is a phrasal verb — that means it is two words (a verb + a preposition/adverb) that work together to create a meaning that is often very different from the individual words. "Hold" alone means to grip something. But "hold up" can mean several different things depending on how it is used. This is one of the most common and useful phrases in English, so understanding all its meanings will serve you very well.

1. To Physically Support Something (Literal Meaning)

This is the most basic, dictionary meaning. When something "holds up" another thing, it supports it from below and prevents it from falling.

Think of it this way: a table holds up your food. Your legs hold up your body.

Examples:

  • "These four pillars hold up the entire roof of the building."
  • "She held up the heavy box while her friend opened the door."
  • "The old shelf couldn't hold up all those books and collapsed."

Key idea: Something is supporting weight from underneath.

2. To Say "Wait!" or "Stop for a Moment" (Exclamation)

This is one of the most common uses in everyday spoken English, especially in informal speech and modern slang. When someone says "Hold up!" on its own — usually quickly, like an exclamation — it means "Wait!" or "Stop what you're doing for a second." It is used when something unexpected happens, or when you need a moment to process information.

Examples:

  • "Hold up! Did you just say you quit your job?" (expressing surprise)
  • "Hold up, hold up — let me make sure I understood that correctly." (asking someone to slow down)
  • "Hold up, I think we made a wrong turn." (pausing to reconsider)

This usage is very common in American English, in casual conversations, and in popular culture. You will hear it frequently in music, movies, and everyday speech. The tone can be surprised, confused, or simply cautious.

Key idea: Pause. Stop. Give me a second.

3. To Cause a Delay (Phrasal Verb)

When something or someone holds you up, it delays you or makes you late. This is a very common usage in everyday life. The thing causing the delay is "holding you up," meaning it is stopping your forward progress.

Examples:

  • "Sorry I'm late — I got held up in traffic."
  • "The bad storm held up the delivery by two days."
  • "What's holding up the project? We should be done by now."
  • "She was held up at the office and missed the train."

Notice that we often say "got held up" (past tense, passive form) when talking about being delayed by something outside our control.

Key idea: Something is blocking your progress and making you wait.

4. To Remain Strong Under Pressure or Over Time (Durability)

When something "holds up," it means it continues to work well, stay strong, or remain valid — even when tested, used heavily, or examined closely. We use this when we want to know if something is truly strong, reliable, or convincing.

This can apply to:

  • Physical objects (will this product last?)
  • Arguments or ideas (is this logic actually correct?)
  • People (is this person coping well?)

Examples:

  • "This old jacket has held up surprisingly well after years of use."
  • "Does your argument hold up when you look at the evidence carefully?"
  • "She held up remarkably well during the most stressful period of her life."
  • "The theory sounded good at first, but it doesn't hold up under serious scrutiny."

The opposite idea would be something that falls apart or breaks down when examined or used.

Key idea: It survived the test — it's still strong, valid, and working.

5. To Rob Someone (Usually at Gunpoint)

In this meaning, to "hold someone up" means to rob them by threatening them, typically with a weapon. The robber "holds up" the victim, forcing them to stop and hand over valuables.

The related noun form is a "holdup" or "hold-up" (written with a hyphen), which refers to the robbery itself.

Examples:

  • "Two masked men held up the bank on Tuesday morning."
  • "She was held up at gunpoint near the subway station."
  • "There was a holdup at the convenience store last night."
  • "The robber held up the cashier and demanded all the money."

This meaning is very well-established in English and is used in news reports, crime stories, films, and everyday conversation.

Key idea: A robbery — usually by force or threat.

6. To Present Someone as an Example or Model

When you "hold someone up" as something, you are publicly presenting or pointing to them as a clear example — usually as a model to admire or follow, though occasionally as a negative example.

Examples:

  • "She was held up as a role model for young scientists everywhere."
  • "The teacher held up his work as an example of excellent writing."
  • "The company was held up as proof that ethical businesses can still succeed."
  • "His failure was held up as a warning to others."

You will almost always see this used in the passive voice ("was held up as"), which is natural in English for this kind of meaning.

Key idea: Pointing to something and saying, "Look at this — this is an example."

When "hold up" is used as a noun, it is usually written as one word ("holdup") or hyphenated ("hold-up"). It has two main noun meanings:

a) A robbery:

  • "There was a holdup at the jewelry store."

b) A delay:

  • "What's the holdup? Why is the line not moving?"
  • "There's a holdup on the highway due to an accident."

So the noun form works the same way as meanings 3 and 5 above, just turned into a thing rather than an action.
How to Know Which Meaning Is Being Used

Since "hold up" has so many meanings, context is everything. Here is a simple way to figure it out:

  • Is someone shouting it quickly alone? → It means "Wait!"
  • Is it about a physical structure supporting weight? → Literal support.
  • Is someone late or delayed? → It means to delay.
  • Is it about whether something is strong, lasting, or convincing? → Durability/endurance.
  • Is there a robbery involved? → It means to rob.
  • Is someone being pointed to as an example? → Presenting as a model.
A Quick Note on Tone and Register

• "Hold up!" (the exclamation) is informal and casual. You would say it to friends or in relaxed situations. In a very formal setting, you might say "Wait a moment" instead.
  • The other meanings (delay, support, durability, robbery, example) are used across both formal and informal English — in news articles, academic writing, and daily conversation alike.
Summary of All Meanings at a Glance

1. Support physically → The poles hold up the tent.
  2. Wait / Pause → "Hold up! What did you say?"
  3. Cause a delay → I got held up at work.
  4. Stay strong / remain valid → The evidence holds up well.
  5. Rob someone → He held up the driver.
  6. Present as an example → She was held up as a genius.
  7. Noun = a robbery or a delay → There was a holdup on the road.

Once you start noticing "hold up" in the wild — in conversations, songs, articles, and films — you will see it pop up constantly in all these forms. The best way to lock these meanings in is to observe each one in real context as you come across it.
7845:
When something holds water, it means it is logically sound, believable, and able to withstand scrutiny — meaning that when you look at it closely and test it, it still makes sense. It still checks out. There are no holes or flaws in it.

When something does not hold water, it means the opposite — the argument, explanation, story, or idea falls apart under examination. It has flaws, weaknesses, or contradictions that make it hard to believe or accept.

Think of it this way: if a bucket holds water, it has no holes — it is solid and reliable. If it doesn't hold water, it has holes, and the water leaks out. Ideas and arguments work the same way in this idiom.

The idiom comes from the literal image of a container holding water. If a pot, bucket, or cup has a crack or a hole in it, water will leak out — it cannot hold water. This simple physical image was borrowed to describe reasoning and logic: just like a leaky bucket cannot keep water inside, a weak argument cannot keep its logic intact when pressure is applied.

This expression has been used in the English language for centuries and is deeply rooted in everyday life, going back to times when people depended on buckets and barrels for carrying water.
The Two Forms You Will See

This idiom almost always appears in one of two forms:

1. "Holds water" (positive)
This means the argument, story, or claim is solid and believable.

"Her explanation holds water. She has receipts, timestamps, and three witnesses."

2. "Doesn't hold water" / "Doesn't hold up" (negative — far more common)
This is the more frequently used form. It means the argument, reasoning, or excuse has flaws that make it unconvincing.

"His alibi doesn't hold water. He said he was home alone, but his car was spotted across the city."
What Kind of Things Can "Hold Water"?

This idiom is used to evaluate the strength or validity of:

  • Arguments — Is the logic in someone's reasoning sound?
  • Excuses — Is the reason someone gives believable?
  • Theories — Does the explanation make sense when examined?
  • Claims and accusations — Is there enough evidence to support what someone is saying?
  • Stories — Does the account someone gives have any contradictions?

Here are examples across different situations so you can see exactly how it works:

In everyday conversation:

"You say you forgot her birthday, but you posted on social media that same day wishing a celebrity happy birthday. That excuse doesn't hold water."

In a courtroom or legal context:

"The defense attorney argued that the prosecution's theory simply doesn't hold water — there is no physical evidence connecting his client to the scene."

In science or academia:

"The old theory that stress directly causes stomach ulcers no longer holds water since we discovered that most ulcers are caused by a bacterium called H. pylori."

In politics:

"The minister's claim that the economy improved because of his policy doesn't hold water — the data shows the improvement began two years before his policy was introduced."

In casual debate:

"Your argument that people work better under pressure might hold water in some jobs, but it clearly doesn't apply to creative fields."
The Feeling and Tone of the Idiom

• It is used in both formal and informal settings.
  • It is neutral in tone — not rude, not overly polite. It is a clean, direct way of challenging or validating an idea.
  • It sounds intelligent and measured. Using it suggests you are someone who tests logic carefully rather than reacting emotionally.
  • The negative form ("doesn't hold water") carries a mild but firm sense of dismissal — you are saying, without being aggressive, that an argument simply isn't good enough.
How It Is Different From Similar Phrases

• "Stand up to scrutiny" — very similar in meaning. Both mean an idea survives being tested. However, "hold water" is more idiomatic and vivid, while "stand up to scrutiny" is more formal.
  • "Hold up" — as in "that story doesn't hold up" — is a shorter, more casual version of the same idea.
  • "Make sense" — simpler and broader. Something can make sense on the surface but still not hold water when you dig deeper. "Hold water" implies a deeper test has been applied.
  • "Add up" — as in "the numbers don't add up." This is similar but is more commonly used for facts, figures, and timelines specifically, while "hold water" is broader and applies to any kind of argument or reasoning.

Some learners mistakenly use this idiom to describe physical things or feelings, like saying "my headache doesn't hold water" — that is incorrect. This idiom is used only for ideas, claims, arguments, stories, theories, or explanations — things that require logic and reasoning to evaluate.

MeaningAn argument or claim is (or isn't) logically sound and believable when examined closely
Most common form"doesn't hold water" — to say something is flawed or unconvincing
Used forArguments, excuses, theories, stories, claims
ToneNeutral, intelligent, firm
OriginA leaky container that cannot keep water inside

The next time someone gives you an excuse that seems weak, or you hear an argument with an obvious flaw, you now have the perfect phrase: "That doesn't hold water." It is precise, clear, and carries real weight in any conversation.
7846: "Hold-up" has two main meanings that are completely different from each other, plus one additional meaning used mainly in British English. Context always makes it clear which one is meant.

A hold-up is a type of robbery where a criminal directly confronts a victim face-to-face, usually with a gun or another weapon, and forces them to hand over money or valuables on the spot.

What makes a hold-up different from other kinds of theft is that it is immediate and threatening. The criminal is right there in front of you. There is no sneaking, no picking pockets, no breaking in secretly at night. The criminal walks up, shows a weapon, and demands you give them what they want — right now.

The most classic example is a bank hold-up, where armed robbers walk into a bank, threaten the staff and customers, and demand cash. But a hold-up can happen anywhere — a convenience store, a gas station, a jewelry shop, or even on the street.

Examples in sentences:

  • "There was a hold-up at the bank on Fifth Avenue this morning — three armed men stole $50,000."
  • "The cashier was terrified during the hold-up but managed to press the silent alarm."
  • "Police are investigating a hold-up at the local post office."

💡 The core idea: A hold-up = an armed, face-to-face robbery where the criminal threatens the victim directly.

A hold-up is also something that slows you down, stops your progress temporarily, or makes you late. It is an obstacle or interruption that prevents things from moving forward as planned.

This is the meaning you will hear far more often in everyday life. Whenever something is taking longer than it should, or when progress has stopped for some reason, people call it a hold-up.

The hold-up can be caused by almost anything — traffic, technical problems, paperwork, bad weather, someone being slow, a missing approval, or an unexpected problem.

Examples in sentences:

  • "Sorry I'm late — there was a hold-up on the highway due to an accident."
  • "There's been a hold-up with the delivery. The package will arrive two days late."
  • "The construction work caused a huge hold-up in traffic this morning."
  • "What's the hold-up? We were supposed to leave an hour ago!" (This last one is a very common expression people use when they're impatient and want to know why there's a delay.)

💡 The core idea: A hold-up = anything that is causing a delay or slowing things down unexpectedly.
Meaning 3: Hold-ups — A Type of Stocking (British English)

In British English, hold-ups (almost always used in the plural) refers to a specific type of women's stockings that stay up on their own without needing a garter belt or any other support. They have an elastic band at the top that grips the leg and keeps them in place. The name makes perfect sense — they hold themselves up.

Example in a sentence:

  • "She bought a pair of hold-ups to go with her evening dress."

💡 Note: This meaning is primarily British, almost always plural, and only appears in clothing-related conversations, so you'll never confuse it with the other two meanings.
You may sometimes see this word written as "holdup" (one word, no hyphen), especially in American English. Both spellings — hold-up and holdup — are correct and mean exactly the same thing.
How to Tell the Three Meanings Apart

Since context always makes this clear, here's a simple guide:

  • Someone talking about crime, a weapon, a bank, or a robbery? → It's a robbery.
  • Someone talking about being late, traffic, waiting, or a slow process? → It's a delay.
  • Someone talking about clothing or women's fashion in a British context? → It's a type of stocking.
7847:
"Hole up" means to hide in a place, or to stay in a place for shelter and safety, usually to avoid something dangerous, uncomfortable, or unpleasant outside.

Think of a small animal — like a rabbit or a fox — that digs itself into a hole in the ground when a predator is nearby. It stays there, hidden and safe, until the danger passes. That is the exact image behind "hole up." When a person "holes up" somewhere, they are doing the human version of that: going into a place and staying there, away from the outside world.

The phrase comes directly from nature. Animals literally hide in holes — burrows, dens, caves — to escape threats. Humans borrowed this image and applied it to their own behavior. Over time, "hole up" became a common everyday expression in English, especially in American English, where it has been used since the 1800s.
What Kind of Phrase It Is

"Hole up" is a phrasal verb — that is, a verb ("hole") combined with a small word ("up") to create a new meaning. The word "hole" here is used as a verb, not a noun. The word "up" does not mean direction (like going upward); instead, it adds the idea of completeness or settling in — the sense that you are getting yourself fully tucked away somewhere.

"Hole up" is used in two closely related ways:

Sense 1 — Hiding from danger, trouble, or people

This is the most classic use. A person or group hides in a location to avoid being found — by enemies, police, danger, or anyone they don't want to face.

"The robbers holed up in an old farmhouse while the police searched the area."

"The spy holed up in a tiny apartment for three weeks to avoid capture."

"The escaped prisoner holed up in the forest until nightfall."

Here, the hiding is usually urgent. There is a real threat outside, and the person is laying low until it passes or until they can safely move.

Sense 2 — Taking shelter from bad conditions

This is a softer, more relaxed use. There is no dramatic enemy — just bad weather, illness, hard work, or simply a wish to be alone. The person goes somewhere and stays put, shut off from the outside world.

"We holed up inside the cabin while the blizzard raged outside."

"She holed up in her bedroom all weekend to finish her novel."

"I was sick, so I holed up at home for a few days."

In this sense, "hole up" carries a slightly cozy or comfortable feeling — the sense of being snug and sheltered while something tough is happening outside.
The Grammar — How to Use It

"Hole up" is almost always used with the preposition "in" to tell people where someone is hiding or sheltering:

"He holed up in a motel on the edge of town."
"They holed up in a bunker."
"She holed up in her office."

You can also use it without a location if the location is already understood from context:

"When the storm hit, we just holed up and waited."

Tense forms:

FormExample
Simple past"They holed up in the mountains."
Present continuous"He is holing up at a friend's house."
Past participle"She has been holed up in her room all day."

The phrase "holed up" (past participle) is very commonly used as a describing phrase:

"The suspect was found holed up in a warehouse."
"She was holed up in the library, surrounded by books."
The Tone and Feeling of the Phrase

"Hole up" is an informal, conversational phrase. You would use it in everyday speech and writing, but you would probably not use it in a formal essay or official document. In formal writing, you might say "sought refuge," "sheltered," or "concealed themselves" instead.

The phrase also carries a strong sense of isolation — the person is cut off from the normal world. It often implies that the stay is temporary: you hole up until the storm ends, the danger passes, or the work is done. You don't "hole up" somewhere forever — that would just be "living" there.

Understanding nearby expressions helps sharpen your sense of exactly what "hole up" means:

"Hide out" — very similar, but it almost always means hiding from people (police, enemies). "Hole up" can be used for hiding from people or from bad weather/conditions.

"The criminals hid out in a basement." ✔

"Hunker down" — means to get into a low, safe position and wait out something difficult. It focuses more on endurance and patience rather than hiding.

"We hunkered down and waited for the hurricane to pass."

"Lay low" — means to keep a very low profile and avoid attention, usually to stay out of trouble. There is no fixed location implied.

"After the argument, he decided to lay low for a while."

"Take cover" — means to quickly get somewhere safe from immediate danger (like gunfire or a storm), but it is more of a sudden, quick action, not a long stay.

"Everyone took cover when the shooting started."

"Hole up" sits between these — it is about going to a specific place and staying there for a while, for either safety or focus, whether the threat is human or environmental.

In a news/crime context:

"Police believe the suspect is holed up somewhere in the city."

In a weather context:

"The hikers holed up in a cave as the thunderstorm rolled in."

In a casual/everyday context:

"I've been holing up at home this week — I just needed a break from everything."

In a historical context:

"During the siege, the soldiers holed up inside the fort for two weeks."

In a work/creative context:

"The author holed up in a remote cottage to write his final chapter."
One Simple Way to Always Remember It

Whenever you hear or see "hole up," picture a fox going into its burrow when it senses a wolf nearby. It disappears inside, stays very still, and waits. That is exactly what "hole up" means — whether the "wolf" is a snowstorm, the police, or just the chaos of everyday life.
7848:
"Holier-than-thou" describes the attitude of a person who behaves as though they are morally better, more virtuous, or more righteous than the people around them. They carry themselves with a sense of moral superiority — quietly (or not so quietly) looking down on others who don't share their values, habits, or standards.

The word is always used critically. It is never a compliment. Calling someone holier-than-thou means you find their moral self-importance irritating, arrogant, and condescending.
Breaking it apart to understand it deeply

The phrase itself tells you everything. "Holier" means "more holy" or "more virtuous." "Than thou" is old-fashioned English for "than you." Literally: "more holy than you." The word packages that smug, superior attitude into a single punchy label.

Now, the crucial insight: a holier-than-thou person doesn't have to actually be morally better than others. They simply act as if they are — and they make sure you feel it. That distinction is the heart of the word. A genuinely good, humble person doesn't lecture you, judge you, or make you feel small. The holier-than-thou person does exactly that.
What it looks like in real life

Imagine someone who decided to stop drinking alcohol. A normal person might simply decline a drink at a party and move on. A holier-than-thou person, however, would sigh loudly, look at your glass with visible disapproval, and say something like, "I honestly don't know how people still drink. I feel so much better about myself now that I've given it up." They're not just making a personal choice — they're making you feel judged for making a different one.

Or consider someone who is very politically active. A holier-than-thou version of that person doesn't just share their views — they treat anyone who disagrees as morally defective, inferior, or simply not as enlightened as they are.

The consistent pattern is this: instead of minding their own life, the holier-than-thou person turns their personal values into a measuring stick they hold up against everyone else — and everyone else always falls short.
The key qualities bundled into this one word

When you call someone holier-than-thou, you're pointing to a combination of attitudes all at once. There is self-righteousness — an unshakeable confidence in their own moral correctness. There is smugness — a calm, self-satisfied sense of being above others. There is preachiness — an urge to lecture, advise, or moralize when nobody asked. And there is condescension — a subtle (or not so subtle) looking-down-upon others.

This is an important nuance. Even though the word uses the word "holy," it is not limited to religious contexts at all. A person can be holier-than-thou about anything they feel morally superior about — their diet, their parenting choices, their environmental habits, their exercise routine, their political beliefs, their financial decisions, their taste in entertainment. Anywhere someone elevates their own choices into a moral standard and judges others against it, the attitude applies.
Does the holier-than-thou person have to be a hypocrite?

Not necessarily, though it often helps explain the irritation people feel. Sometimes a holier-than-thou person genuinely follows the values they preach — they really do eat perfectly, exercise daily, and volunteer on weekends. But they still earn the label because of how they behave about it: making others feel inferior, passing judgment, and treating their personal choices as the only correct ones. The problem isn't what they believe — it's the arrogance and condescension with which they wear it.

It works to describe a person, an attitude, a tone, or even the way something sounds. For example: "She has such a holier-than-thou attitude about organic food — she makes everyone at the table feel guilty." Or: "His holier-than-thou tone during the debate turned people off immediately." Or: "Stop being so holier-than-thou — I didn't ask for your opinion on my choices." Or: "The article was informative, but it had a holier-than-thou edge to it."

Three words are close relatives and knowing them deepens your understanding. Self-righteous is the nearest synonym — it means the same smug certainty in one's own moral superiority. Sanctimonious (more formal) means making an exaggerated, performative show of being morally upright, often to impress others. Preachy focuses specifically on the lecturing, moralizing aspect. "Holier-than-thou" essentially captures all three at once — the self-satisfaction of self-righteousness, the performance of sanctimony, and the unsolicited lecturing of preachiness — which is why it's such a loaded and vivid word.

It does not mean simply having strong values or high standards — a person can hold firm beliefs without ever making others feel judged. It does not mean being religious or devout — a deeply religious person who is humble and kind would never be described this way. And it does not mean being strict — someone can be strict with themselves while staying completely non-judgmental toward others. The word only applies when the superiority is performed outwardly and directed at others.
If you ever need to recall the meaning quickly: a holier-than-thou person is someone who treats their own morality as proof that they are better than you — and makes sure you know it.
7849:
Holistic means looking at, treating, or understanding something as a complete whole — considering all of its parts together, along with how those parts connect and affect each other — rather than focusing on just one piece at a time in isolation.

The central idea is this: the whole is more than just the sum of its parts. A holistic thinker believes that to truly understand something, you cannot just examine its individual pieces one by one. You must step back and look at the entire picture — how everything fits together, how the parts influence each other, and how the bigger context shapes the thing you're trying to understand.

To understand "holistic" deeply, it helps to know what it stands against.

The opposite of a holistic approach is a narrow or fragmented approach — one that zooms in on a single part, ignores everything else, and treats that part as if it exists in a vacuum.

Think of it like this:

Imagine a tree is dying. A narrow approach looks only at the leaves — they're brown, so it concludes the leaves are the problem. A holistic approach looks at the leaves and the roots, the soil, the amount of sunlight, the water supply, nearby plants, and recent weather. It understands that the dying leaves are a symptom, and that the real cause might be something else entirely — possibly a combination of several things working together.
Everyday Examples to Cement the Meaning

In medicine:
A doctor using a holistic approach to treat a patient's chronic headaches won't just prescribe painkillers and move on. Instead, they will examine the person's sleep habits, stress levels, diet, posture, emotional wellbeing, work environment, and physical health — all together — because they understand that the human body is an interconnected system. A problem in one area often shows up as a symptom in another.

In education:
A holistic approach to educating a child doesn't only focus on test scores and academic grades. It also nurtures the child's emotional intelligence, social skills, physical health, creativity, and sense of self-worth — because a truly well-educated person needs all of these things working together.

In the workplace:
If a company's productivity is dropping, a holistic approach doesn't just blame employee laziness or demand longer working hours. It examines everything: company culture, management style, employee workload, available resources, communication patterns, team morale, and the clarity of goals — because the solution is likely somewhere in the interaction between all these factors.

In everyday thinking:
If your friend asks why they're always feeling tired, a holistic answer might explore their sleep, exercise routine, diet, stress, screen time, social life, and purpose in life — not just one of these things in isolation.

When something is described as holistic, it has these qualities:

It's inclusive. It does not cherry-pick only the convenient or obvious parts. It deliberately brings in all relevant aspects, even ones that seem indirect or unrelated at first.

It's interconnected. It recognizes that the parts of a system affect each other. Changing one thing ripples through and affects other things.

It's context-aware. It understands that something cannot be fully understood without knowing its wider environment and circumstances.

It resists oversimplification. A holistic thinker is uncomfortable with quick, one-dimensional answers to complex problems, because they know that real-world things are rarely that simple.

The word "holistic" is almost always paired with a noun to describe a particular type of whole-picture thinking:

  • Holistic approach — a way of tackling a problem by considering all its dimensions at once
  • Holistic view / perspective — seeing the big picture rather than fixating on one part
  • Holistic health / medicine — treating the entire person (body, mind, emotions, lifestyle) not just a disease
  • Holistic education — developing every dimension of a student, not just academic performance
  • Holistic assessment — evaluating someone or something by looking at the full range of factors, not just one metric
  • Holistic thinking — a mode of reasoning that always asks "how does this fit into the larger whole?"

If you ever need to recall the word quickly:

Holistic = considering or dealing with the whole of something — all its parts, connections, and context — rather than any single piece in isolation.
A Good Way to Remember It

Think of the word as being built around the idea of "whole." Holistic thinking is whole-picture thinking. Whenever you see this word, ask yourself: who or what is being looked at completely, rather than partially? That's your answer.
